Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management: Three customer-managed KMS keys are provisioned with distinct scopes: data tier (EBS volumes, RDS, ElastiCache, S3), secrets tier (Secrets Manager), and logs tier (CloudWatch). Each key has automatic annual rotation enabled. Key deletion requires a 30-day waiting period (configurable 7-30 days), preventing accidental key destruction that would render encrypted data irrecoverable. Key policies restrict usage to specific AWS service principals via kms:ViaService conditions. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000514, FedRAMP SC-12.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: aws_kms_key.data, aws_kms_key.secrets, aws_kms_key.logs with enable_key_rotation=true, deletion_window_in_days=30.

by-components.description: Shared responsibility with AWS CSP. AWS provides the platform capability (FedRAMP authorized infrastructure). The customer (SPARC) configures, monitors, and documents use through Terraform IaC and/or application controls. Parts: SC-12. Customer responsibility: AWS customers are responsible for establishing and managing cryptographic keys for required cryptography employed within their system in accordance with organization-defined requirements for key generation, distribution, storage, access, and destruction.

Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management | Availability: KMS keys are regional resources backed by FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSMs. Key material cannot be exported. Automatic key rotation creates new cryptographic material annually while retaining old material for decryption of existing data. The 30-day deletion window provides recovery time if a key is scheduled for deletion. Multi-region keys are disabled to maintain key locality within the deployment region. Reference: FedRAMP SC-12(1).
by-components.remarks: AWS KMS uses FIPS 140-2 Level 3 HSMs. multi_region=false ensures keys stay in the deployment region.

by-components.description: Cryptographic Protection: All KMS keys use AES-256-GCM symmetric encryption via AWS KMS HSMs. Key policies enforce that cryptographic operations (Encrypt, Decrypt, ReEncrypt, GenerateDataKey) can only be performed by authorized AWS service principals from the deployment account. The kms:CallerAccount condition prevents cross-account usage. The kms:ViaService condition restricts each key to its designated services only. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000179, FedRAMP SC-13.
by-components.remarks: Key policies use StringEquals conditions for kms:ViaService and kms:CallerAccount. Logs key uses ArnLike condition for CloudWatch service principal.

by-components.description: Shared responsibility with AWS CSP. AWS provides the platform capability (FedRAMP authorized infrastructure). The customer (SPARC) configures, monitors, and documents use through Terraform IaC and/or application controls. Parts: SC-13.a, SC-13.b. Customer responsibility: AWS customers are responsible for determining the [Assignment: organization-defined cryptographic uses].

Public Key Infrastructure Certificates: ACM certificates are issued by the Amazon Trust Services CA, which is trusted by all major browsers and operating systems. Certificate transparency logging is enabled by default, publishing all issued certificates to public CT logs for auditability. Subject Alternative Names (SANs) are configurable. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000514.
by-components.remarks: SANs are configurable via the certificate_san variable. ACM certificates appear in Certificate Transparency logs.

by-components.description: Shared responsibility with AWS CSP. AWS provides the platform capability (FedRAMP authorized infrastructure). The customer (SPARC) configures, monitors, and documents use through Terraform IaC and/or application controls. Parts: SC-17.a, SC-17.b. Customer responsibility: AWS customers are responsible for issuing public key certificates under an organization-defined certificate policy or obtaining public key certificates from an approved service provider.

Secure Name/Address Resolution Service (Authoritative Source): Route 53 provides authoritative DNS resolution for the application domain. Route 53 supports DNSSEC signing for hosted zones, enabling cryptographic validation of DNS responses to prevent spoofing and cache poisoning. The A record alias maps the user-facing domain directly to the ALB, ensuring clients resolve to the correct endpoint. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000131, CIS AWS 2.7.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_route53_record.app (A record alias). Consider enabling DNSSEC signing on the hosted zone for full SC-20 compliance.

by-components.description: Shared responsibility with AWS CSP. AWS provides the platform capability (FedRAMP authorized infrastructure). The customer (SPARC) configures, monitors, and documents use through Terraform IaC and/or application controls. Parts: SC-20.a, SC-20.b. Customer responsibility: AWS customers are responsible for providing additional data origin authentication and integrity verification artifacts along with the authoritative name resolution data the system returns in response to external name/address resolution queries.

Secure Name/Address Resolution Service (Recursive or Caching Resolver): Route 53 Resolver provides recursive DNS resolution for resources within the VPC. DNS queries from ECS tasks in private subnets are resolved through the VPC DNS resolver (AmazonProvidedDNS), which validates responses and prevents DNS-based attacks within the network boundary. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000132.
by-components.remarks: VPC DNS support is enabled (enable_dns_support = true) in the networking module. Private subnet resources use the VPC resolver for both internal and external name resolution.

by-components.description: Shared responsibility with AWS CSP. AWS provides the platform capability (FedRAMP authorized infrastructure). The customer (SPARC) configures, monitors, and documents use through Terraform IaC and/or application controls. Parts: SC-21. Customer responsibility: AWS customers are responsible for configuring their systems to perform data origin authentication and data integrity verification on DNS resolution responses received from authoritative sources.

Architecture and Provisioning for Name/Address Resolution Service: Route 53 is a globally distributed, highly available DNS service with a 100% uptime SLA. DNS resolution is fault-tolerant by design — Route 53 operates across multiple AWS edge locations worldwide. The alias record uses evaluate_target_health = true, ensuring DNS only resolves to healthy ALB endpoints. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000133.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_route53_record.app with alias evaluate_target_health = true. Route 53 provides built-in DDoS protection for DNS queries via AWS Shield.

by-components.description: Shared responsibility with AWS CSP. AWS provides the platform capability (FedRAMP authorized infrastructure). The customer (SPARC) configures, monitors, and documents use through Terraform IaC and/or application controls. Parts: SC-22. Customer responsibility: AWS customers are responsible for ensuring that information systems collectively providing name resolution services to their organization are fault-tolerant and have implemented internal/external role separation.

Shared responsibility with AWS CSP. AWS provides the platform capability (FedRAMP authorized infrastructure). The customer (SPARC) configures, monitors, and documents use through Terraform IaC and/or application controls. Parts: SC-23. Customer responsibility: AWS customers are responsible for configuring their systems to protect the authenticity of communications sessions.
Config rules encrypted-volumes and rds-storage-encrypted continuously verify that data-at-rest encryption is enabled on EBS and RDS resources.

Protection of Information at Rest: ECR repositories use AES-256 server-side encryption for all stored images. Container layers and manifests are encrypted at rest in the AWS-managed storage backend. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000231.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_ecr_repository.main with encryption_configuration.encryption_type = AES256. Consider KMS CMK for additional control.

by-components.description: Protection of Information at Rest: Two Secrets Manager secrets are injected at runtime: DB_CREDENTIALS (database connection details) and APP_SECRETS (SECRET_KEY_BASE, OIDC client secrets, LDAP bind password, SMTP password, and all SPARC configuration). DATABASE_URL and REDIS_URL are injected as environment variables. No credentials are stored in task definitions, images, or source code. Secrets Manager encrypts all values at rest with AWS KMS. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000231.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: secrets block in container_definitions referencing module.rds.db_secret_arn and module.secrets.app_secret_arn.

by-components.description: Protection of Information at Rest: At-rest encryption is enabled (at_rest_encryption_enabled = true), encrypting all data persisted to disk including RDB snapshots and AOF logs. Encryption uses AWS-managed keys. This protects session tokens, cached data, and any SPARC application state stored in Redis. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000231.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_elasticache_replication_group.main with at_rest_encryption_enabled = true.

by-components.description: Protection of Information at Rest: CMKs provide organization-controlled encryption for all data at rest across the stack. The data key encrypts EBS volumes (OS + app data), RDS storage and Performance Insights, ElastiCache at-rest data, and S3 objects. The secrets key encrypts all Secrets Manager values (DB credentials, SECRET_KEY_BASE, OIDC/LDAP/SMTP secrets). The logs key encrypts CloudWatch log groups (VPC flow logs, application logs). This tiered approach ensures SPARC compliance data (SAP, SAR, POAM, profiles, validation) is protected with customer-controlled keys. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000231, FedRAMP SC-28(1).
by-components.remarks: Three keys by data classification: data (compute/storage), secrets (credentials/config), logs (audit trails). All wired via kms_key_arn variables.

by-components.description: Protection of Information at Rest: RDS storage encryption is enabled (storage_encrypted = true), using AWS-managed KMS keys to encrypt all data, logs, backups, and snapshots at rest. This ensures data confidentiality even if physical storage media is compromised. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000231, CIS AWS 2.3.1.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_db_instance.main with storage_encrypted = true. Consider using a customer-managed KMS key (kms_key_id) for additional control.

by-components.description: Protection of Information at Rest: S3 bucket uses AWS KMS server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) with bucket key enabled for all stored objects. Every uploaded file is automatically encrypted before being written to disk. Encryption is enforced — unencrypted uploads are rejected. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000231, CIS AWS 2.1.1.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration.uploads with sse_algorithm = aws:kms.

by-components.description: Protection of Information at Rest: All application secrets are encrypted at rest using AWS KMS within Secrets Manager. This includes SECRET_KEY_BASE, OIDC client secrets, LDAP bind password, and SMTP password. Secrets are never written to disk in plaintext — they are injected into ECS tasks at runtime via the Secrets Manager integration. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000231.
by-components.remarks: Secrets Manager uses AES-256 encryption via KMS. Consider using a customer-managed KMS key for additional control over encryption key lifecycle.

by-components.description: Protection of Information at Rest: The SNS topic is encrypted using AWS-managed KMS key (kms_master_key_id=alias/aws/sns). All messages published to the topic (alarm notifications containing infrastructure metrics and alert details) are encrypted at rest before delivery. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000231.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_sns_topic.alarms with kms_master_key_id = alias/aws/sns.

by-components.description: Shared responsibility with AWS CSP. AWS provides the platform capability (FedRAMP authorized infrastructure). The customer (SPARC) configures, monitors, and documents use through Terraform IaC and/or application controls. Parts: SC-28. Customer responsibility: AWS customers are responsible for configuring their systems to protect the confidentiality and/or integrity of organization-defined information at rest in accordance with their system and communications protection policy.

Denial-of-Service Protection: AWS ALB provides built-in DDoS protection via AWS Shield Standard (included at no cost). The ALB distributes incoming traffic across multiple ECS tasks in private subnets, preventing single-point-of-failure. Consider adding AWS WAF for application-layer protection. Reference: CIS AWS 6.1.
by-components.remarks: For enhanced protection, attach AWS WAF WebACL and enable AWS Shield Advanced.

by-components.description: Denial-of-Service Protection: ECS auto-scaling (enable_autoscaling=true) automatically adjusts task count based on CPU utilization and ALB request count per target. Scale-out responds to traffic spikes within 300 seconds; scale-in has a 600-second cooldown to prevent flapping. Minimum task count ensures baseline capacity. Combined with ALB distribution and AWS Shield Standard, this provides layered DoS mitigation. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000362.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: aws_appautoscaling_target.ecs, aws_appautoscaling_policy.cpu (target: 70%), aws_appautoscaling_policy.requests (target: 1000/target). Conditional on enable_autoscaling variable.

by-components.description: Denial-of-Service Protection: NGINX provides request buffering (proxy_buffering on, proxy_buffer_size 8k, proxy_buffers 16 8k) to protect Rails from slow clients. The client_max_body_size 100m limit prevents oversized request attacks. Proxy timeouts (60s connect/send/read) prevent connection exhaustion. Gzip compression reduces bandwidth consumption. Combined with ALB connection limits and AWS Shield Standard, this provides layered DoS protection. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000362.
by-components.remarks: Buffering, body size limits, and timeouts in conf.d/default.conf. Gzip configuration in nginx.conf.

by-components.description: Boundary Protection: The ALB drops invalid HTTP headers (drop_invalid_header_fields=true), preventing header injection attacks from reaching backend services. Deletion protection is enabled (enable_deletion_protection=true), preventing accidental or unauthorized removal of the network boundary. Access logging is configurable via an S3 bucket for forensic analysis of all requests. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000364.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_lb.main with drop_invalid_header_fields=true, enable_deletion_protection=true, access_logs block.

by-components.description: Boundary Protection: VPC flow logs monitor all traffic crossing network boundaries within the VPC, including traffic between security groups (ALB→ECS, ECS→RDS, ECS→Redis). Rejected traffic is logged, providing visibility into unauthorized access attempts. Flow logs capture traffic that security groups deny, enabling detection of reconnaissance and lateral movement attempts. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000364.
by-components.remarks: Flow logs capture ALL traffic types (accept + reject). Log group retention is configurable (default 30 days) for compliance requirements.

by-components.description: Boundary Protection: The sidecar architecture provides defense in depth. External traffic enters through NGINX on port 8080 (ALB-facing). Rails/Puma on port 3000 is only accessible via localhost within the task — it has no external port mapping. NGINX enforces request buffering, size limits (client_max_body_size 100m), and proper header forwarding (X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Port). Dotfiles and hidden paths are denied at the NGINX layer. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000364.
by-components.remarks: NGINX conf.d/default.conf proxies to 127.0.0.1:3000. Rails port 3000 is not in the ECS service load_balancer block — only NGINX port 8080 is registered with the ALB target group.

by-components.description: Boundary Protection: Redis is deployed in private subnets via a dedicated subnet group. The Redis security group permits inbound connections exclusively on port 6379 from the ECS security group. No public endpoint is configured. Redis is not accessible from the internet or any other VPC resource. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000364.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: aws_elasticache_subnet_group.main (private subnets), aws_security_group.redis (ECS-only ingress) in networking module.

by-components.description: Runtime monitoring detects malicious network activity from within containers — complements VPC flow logs and security group enforcement.

Boundary Protection: NGINX serves as the application-layer boundary between the ALB and Rails. It accepts connections only on port 8080 from the ALB and forwards to Rails on 127.0.0.1:3000 (not network-accessible). NGINX denies access to dotfiles and hidden paths (location ~ /\.). The client_max_body_size directive (100m) limits request body size, preventing oversized upload attacks. NGINX enforces proxy timeouts (connect: 60s, send: 60s, read: 60s). Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000364, SRG-APP-000141.
by-components.remarks: Configuration: nginx/conf.d/default.conf. Dotfile denial, body size limits, and timeout enforcement are in the server block.

by-components.description: Boundary Protection: The RDS instance is deployed in a DB subnet group spanning private subnets only. The RDS security group permits inbound connections exclusively from the ECS security group on port 5432. No public IP is assigned and no internet gateway route exists for the private subnets. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000364.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: aws_db_subnet_group.main (private subnets), aws_security_group.rds (ECS-only ingress).

by-components.description: Boundary Protection: The DNS record serves as the entry point to the application boundary. Only the ALB endpoint is exposed via DNS — no internal resources (ECS tasks, RDS instances) have public DNS records. The alias record routes traffic exclusively to the ALB, which enforces the network boundary via security groups and TLS termination. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000364.
by-components.remarks: The Route 53 module is conditionally deployed only when hosted_zone_id and domain_name are provided, allowing ALB-only deployments without DNS.

by-components.description: Boundary Protection: The VPC establishes a network boundary with public subnets (ALB-facing) isolated from private subnets (ECS tasks, RDS, Redis). Public subnets have map_public_ip_on_launch disabled, ensuring instances launched in public subnets do not automatically receive public IP addresses — only the ALB receives a public-facing endpoint. Four security groups enforce layered ingress rules: ALB SG permits 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0, ECS SG permits container_port from ALB SG only, RDS SG permits 5432 from ECS SG only, Redis SG permits 6379 from ECS SG only. No direct internet access to private subnets. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000364, CIS AWS 5.1, CIS AWS 5.2.1.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: aws_vpc.main, aws_subnet.public (map_public_ip_on_launch = false), aws_subnet.private, aws_security_group.alb, aws_security_group.ecs, aws_security_group.rds, aws_security_group.redis

by-components.description: Boundary Protection | Isolation of System Components: ECS tasks and RDS instances are deployed into private subnets with no public IP addresses. Public subnets also disable automatic public IP assignment (map_public_ip_on_launch = false), ensuring no resources receive unintended public exposure. Internet-facing traffic is isolated to the ALB in public subnets via its own Elastic IP/public DNS. Subnet-level separation provides network isolation between application and data tiers.
by-components.remarks: Private subnets have no internet gateway route; outbound traffic routes through NAT gateway. Public subnets have map_public_ip_on_launch = false.

by-components.description: Boundary Protection | Deny by Default / Allow by Exception: Security groups default-deny all inbound traffic. Only explicitly defined ingress rules are permitted: HTTP/HTTPS to ALB, container port from ALB to ECS, PostgreSQL from ECS to RDS, Redis from ECS to ElastiCache. Egress is allowed for operational connectivity (NAT gateway for ECS outbound). Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000202.
by-components.remarks: All four security groups (ALB, ECS, RDS, Redis) are created in the networking module to prevent circular dependencies between downstream modules.

by-components.description: Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity: ACM provisions and manages X.509 TLS certificates used by the ALB to encrypt all client-facing traffic. Certificates are validated via DNS (Route 53 CNAME records), proving domain ownership. ACM handles automatic renewal before expiration, preventing certificate lapses. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000062, CIS AWS 2.1.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: aws_acm_certificate.main (DNS validation), aws_route53_record.validation, aws_acm_certificate_validation.main.

by-components.description: Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity: All external client traffic is encrypted via TLS. The HTTPS listener on port 443 uses an ACM-managed certificate with TLS 1.3 policy (ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06). HTTP requests on port 80 receive a 301 redirect to HTTPS, ensuring no unencrypted client communication. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000062, CIS AWS 2.1.2.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: aws_lb_listener.https (TLS termination), aws_lb_listener.http_redirect (301 redirect). TLS policy enforces TLS 1.2 minimum with TLS 1.3 preferred.

by-components.description: Config rule s3-bucket-ssl-requests-only verifies that S3 buckets require HTTPS for all requests, protecting data in transit.

Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity: In-transit encryption is enabled (transit_encryption_enabled = true), requiring TLS for all connections between ECS tasks and Redis. The REDIS_URL uses the rediss:// scheme (TLS) rather than redis:// (plaintext). This protects session data and cached content from network interception. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000062, CIS AWS 3.4.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_elasticache_replication_group.main with transit_encryption_enabled = true. Application connects via rediss:// URL.

by-components.description: Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity: NGINX forwards security-relevant headers from the ALB to Rails: X-Forwarded-Proto (ensures Rails knows the original protocol is HTTPS), X-Forwarded-For (preserves client IP through the proxy chain), X-Real-IP (direct client address), and X-Forwarded-Port. Rails uses X-Forwarded-Proto to enforce FORCE_SSL=true. Internal traffic between NGINX and Rails is on localhost (127.0.0.1) within the same Fargate task — no network traversal. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000062.
by-components.remarks: Header configuration in conf.d/default.conf proxy_set_header directives. TLS termination happens at the ALB; NGINX receives plaintext from the ALB.

by-components.description: Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity: The DNS alias record directs clients to the ALB, which enforces HTTPS. While standard DNS queries are unencrypted, Route 53 supports DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) via Route 53 Resolver endpoints for internal resolution. The end-to-end flow is: DNS resolution (Route 53) → HTTPS connection (ALB with TLS 1.3) → application. Reference: DISA SRG-NET-000062.
by-components.remarks: DNS resolution itself is not encrypted by default. For sensitive environments, consider Route 53 Resolver with DoH endpoints and DNSSEC signing.

by-components.description: Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity: An S3 bucket policy enforces SSL/TLS for all bucket access by denying any request where aws:SecureTransport is false. This ensures all data in transit to and from the S3 bucket is encrypted, preventing interception of uploaded files and application data. The same SSL-only policy is applied to the logging module's artifacts bucket. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000439, CIS AWS 2.1.2.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: aws_s3_bucket_policy.uploads_ssl_only (S3 module), aws_s3_bucket_policy.artifacts_ssl_only (logging module). Both use Condition: {Bool: {aws:SecureTransport: false}} with Effect: Deny.

by-components.description: Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Cryptographic Protection: ACM certificates use RSA 2048-bit keys minimum. Private keys are generated and stored within AWS Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) — they cannot be exported or accessed directly. Certificate lifecycle (issuance, renewal, revocation) is fully managed by AWS. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000014.
by-components.remarks: ACM private keys never leave AWS HSMs. The create_before_destroy lifecycle ensures zero-downtime certificate rotation.

by-components.description: Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Cryptographic Protection: ALB uses AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for TLS certificate provisioning and automatic rotation. The ssl_policy ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 enforces strong cipher suites and disables deprecated protocols (SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1). Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000014.
by-components.remarks: Certificate ARN is provided via the certificate_arn variable. ACM handles certificate renewal automatically.

by-components.description: Information Input Validation: ALB health checks validate application availability by checking the /nginx-health endpoint on the NGINX sidecar container. This lightweight endpoint returns HTTP 200 without proxying to Rails, verifying that the reverse proxy layer is functional. Unhealthy targets are automatically removed from the target group rotation. The ALB routes to the NGINX container (port 8080), which then proxies to Rails (port 3000 on localhost).
by-components.remarks: Health check settings: interval=30s, healthy_threshold=3, unhealthy_threshold=3, timeout=5s, matcher=200, path=/nginx-health. ALB target group uses IP type (Fargate requirement) and targets the NGINX container.

by-components.description: Information Input Validation: NGINX provides a dedicated health check endpoint (/nginx-health) that returns HTTP 200 with a plain text response without proxying to Rails. This allows the ALB to verify NGINX availability independently. The ALB target group health check is configured to hit /nginx-health, ensuring the reverse proxy layer is functional before routing traffic. Unhealthy tasks (where NGINX is down) are automatically deregistered. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000251.
by-components.remarks: Health check in conf.d/default.conf: location /nginx-health returns 200. ALB health_check_path defaults to /nginx-health.

by-components.description: Semgrep enforces input validation rules on Python scripts that process external data (Checkov JSON, YAML baselines, OSCAL documents). Rules detect command injection, path traversal, and unsafe deserialization patterns.

Shared responsibility with AWS CSP. AWS provides the platform capability (FedRAMP authorized infrastructure). The customer (SPARC) configures, monitors, and documents use through Terraform IaC and/or application controls. Parts: SI-10. Customer responsibility: AWS customers are responsible for configuring their systems to check the validity of organization-defined inputs.

Flaw Remediation: Scan-on-push findings highlight known vulnerabilities in container images, enabling remediation before or during deployment. The lifecycle policy automatically expires old images, reducing the attack surface from unpatched historical versions. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000456.
by-components.remarks: Integrate ECR scan findings with CI/CD pipelines to prevent deployment of images with critical/high vulnerabilities.

by-components.description: pip-audit scans Python dependency manifests (requirements.txt) against the Python Packaging Advisory Database for known vulnerabilities. Findings are reported in SARIF format, converted to HDF, and included in OSCAL Assessment Results for continuous flaw tracking.

Flaw Remediation: Auto minor version upgrade is enabled (auto_minor_version_upgrade=true), ensuring the RDS instance automatically receives security patches and bug fixes during maintenance windows. This reduces the window of exposure to known PostgreSQL vulnerabilities without requiring manual intervention. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000456.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resource: aws_db_instance.main with auto_minor_version_upgrade=true. Major version upgrades still require manual action.

by-components.description: Malicious Code Protection: ECR scan-on-push is enabled (scan_on_push = true) on both the application and NGINX repositories, automatically scanning every pushed image for known CVEs using the Amazon Inspector scanning engine. Scan findings are available via the ECR console and API, enabling CI/CD pipelines to gate deployments on vulnerability severity. Both images are scanned independently. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000277, CIS AWS 2.1.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: aws_ecr_repository.main (app) and aws_ecr_repository.nginx (sidecar), both with image_scanning_configuration.scan_on_push = true.

by-components.description: Malicious Code Protection: Fargate runs containers in isolated Firecracker micro-VMs with per-task kernel isolation. Both the NGINX and Rails container images are scanned on push to ECR (scan_on_push = true). The NGINX image is built from a minimal Alpine base (nginx:1.27-alpine) with only the required configuration files. Image tag immutability prevents unauthorized image replacement. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000277.
by-components.remarks: ECR scan-on-push covers both app and nginx repositories. NGINX Dockerfile copies only nginx.conf and conf.d/default.conf — no application code.

by-components.description: Semgrep SAST scanning detects injection vulnerabilities, cross-site scripting, path traversal, and other malicious code patterns in Python scripts that handle security data (OSCAL assembly, Checkov analysis, compliance packaging). Findings block merges via the security gate when thresholds are exceeded.

System Monitoring: 13 CloudWatch alarms provide continuous automated monitoring across all infrastructure tiers: ECS (CPU high, memory high), ALB (5xx errors, latency high, unhealthy targets), RDS (CPU high, storage low, connections high), ElastiCache (CPU high, memory high), and application (NGINX 5xx rate, Rails error rate). All alarms use configurable thresholds, evaluate over multiple periods to avoid false positives, and treat missing data as not-breaching. All alarms are configured with alarm_actions, ok_actions, and insufficient_data_actions, ensuring SNS notifications are sent for all state transitions including when metrics become unavailable. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000029, CIS AWS 4.1.
by-components.remarks: Alarms use 5-minute periods with 2-3 evaluation periods. Thresholds are configurable via root Terraform variables. All 13 alarms notify on ALARM, OK, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA states.

by-components.description: AWS Config monitors system configuration for security-relevant changes. VPC flow logs, CloudTrail, and Config together provide comprehensive monitoring coverage.

GuardDuty provides continuous runtime monitoring of ECS Fargate containers. Detects crypto mining, container escape, malicious DNS queries, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access patterns. Agent auto-injected by AWS — no task definition changes.

System Monitoring: SNS is the notification backbone for the monitoring stack. All 12 CloudWatch alarms publish to the SNS topic when thresholds are breached or when alarms return to OK state. This provides continuous monitoring coverage across all infrastructure tiers: compute (ECS), networking (ALB), data (RDS, Redis), and application (log-derived metrics). Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000029, CIS AWS 4.1.
by-components.remarks: SNS topic policy explicitly allows cloudwatch.amazonaws.com to publish. Both alarm and ok actions route to the same topic.

by-components.description: This control is fully inherited from the AWS Cloud Service Provider (CSP) under the AWS FedRAMP authorization (US East/West — Moderate, GovCloud — High). AWS is responsible for implementing and maintaining this control for all infrastructure and physical security aspects. Parts: SI-04(14). Customer note: This control is inheritable as long as the customer system is hosted exclusively in AWS FedRAMP-authorized Regions.
EventBridge rule routes MEDIUM+ severity findings (>= 4.0) to a dedicated SNS topic for email notification. Severity scale: LOW (1-3.9), MEDIUM (4-6.9), HIGH (7-8.9), CRITICAL (9-10).

Security Alerts, Advisories, and Directives: All 13 CloudWatch alarms are configured with insufficient_data_actions in addition to alarm_actions and ok_actions, ensuring SNS notifications are triggered when metric data becomes unavailable. This prevents silent monitoring gaps — operators are alerted when alarms enter the INSUFFICIENT_DATA state, which may indicate a logging pipeline failure, a stopped resource, or a configuration issue requiring investigation. Reference: DISA SRG-APP-000516.
by-components.remarks: Terraform resources: all aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm resources include insufficient_data_actions = [aws_sns_topic.alerts.arn]. This complements alarm_actions and ok_actions for full state-transition coverage.
